summary:
Earthify turns NASA climate data into a detective game. Reading about climate change in textbooks is dry, so we wanted people, especially school students, to find the trends themselves.

Our app shows a 3D globe coloured with NASA MERRA-2 data from 1981 to 2025. Temperature, rain, soil moisture, sea ice, snow, air pollution and nine more layers, down to grid cells of roughly 100 km. In Game Mode, you get clues about a secret place, like “It's gotten a lot hotter here over the last 40 years.”. Explore the layers on the globe, drop pins where you think it might be, and make your guess! Points depend on distance and speed. A short quiz afterwards shows what these changes mean for the people living there.

In free mode you can tap any country or ocean region and see its long-term trend, whether it is statistically significant, and where it would be in 2040 if it kept going. Blob, our AI guide, answers questions and can operate the map, for example to compare two countries.

This is what the challenge asks for: users don't just look at data, they detect trends, check if they are real and learn what they mean. That makes climate data stick and people aware of climate change.
details:
Our mission
Most people learn about climate change from charts that already give them the answer. They read it, nod, and forget it. We think climate trends stick much better when you have to find them yourself. So we built Earthify as a game. You play a detective, and to win you have to read real NASA data: where it’s getting warmer, where the soil is drying out, where the sea ice is gone. You learn the trends while you play. Our main audience is school students, but anyone can join.

How the game teaches
Each round is about a secret place somewhere on Earth. You get clues one layer at a time, for example “It’s gotten a lot hotter here over the last 40 years.” To find the place, you look at the 3D globe, switch between layers and compare regions. You drop pins and then lock in your final guess. Points depend on how close you are and how fast you were, so there’s a reason to look carefully and quickly.

Most of the learning happens after the guess:

  • Reveal: your pin is compared with the real trends, layer by layer. You see why the answer was right or where you went wrong.
  • Impact quiz: a few questions on what these changes mean for the people living there, such as drought in the Amazon, floods in Bangladesh or dust storms in the Sahel. Every answer links to its source.
  • Next round: a new place with other layers. After a few rounds you start to spot patterns yourself, like the Arctic warming faster than anywhere else.

So the loop is: guess, check, understand, play again. One round takes a few minutes, which fits easily into a school lesson.

Free Mode and Blob
If you get curious, you can switch to Free Mode. Tap any country, city or ocean region and see its trend since 1981, whether it’s statistically significant and where it would be in 2040 if it continued. Blob, our star mascot, guides new players through a hands-on tutorial, gives hints during the game and answers questions by text or voice. He can also control the map for you, for example “compare Germany and Spain”.

Real data, told honestly
Everything is based on NASA MERRA-2 reanalysis data from 1981 to 2025: 15 layers on a grid of about 100 km, covering roughly 2,700 regions. Our Python pipeline calculates the trends (Sen’s slope) and checks whether they are significant (Seasonal Mann-Kendall test). If a trend isn’t significant, the app says so. The 2040 values are clearly marked as a continued trend, not a climate model. The app is built with React, TypeScript and react-globe.gl/three.js. Blob runs on a small Node server that uses the Claude API, and voice mode uses Deepgram.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

  • We used Claude (Anthropic) as an SI coding assistant
  • Blob’s answers are SI-generated live by the Claude API, and his voice is SI-synthesised with Deepgram Aura-2.
  • All data, statistics and quiz facts come from the listed sources, not from the SI tools.
